stem: Define vital capacity. What is its significance?
solution:
**Vital capacity (VC)** is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, or the maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a forced inspiration. It includes **ERV, TV and IRV** (VC = ERV + TV + IRV), i.e., about 1000-1100 mL + 500 mL + 2500-3000 mL = approximately **4000-4600 mL**.

**Significance:**

1. It is the largest volume of air that can be renewed in the lungs in one breath, so it indicates the strength of breathing and the efficiency of the lungs.
2. Like other pulmonary capacities, it is measured with a **spirometer** and is used in the **clinical assessment of pulmonary functions** and in clinical diagnosis.
3. A higher vital capacity means more air is exchanged per breath; it is higher in athletes.
groundedIn: §14.2.1; §14.2 — VC is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, includes ERV, TV and IRV; TV approx. 500 mL, IRV 2500-3000 mL, ERV 1000-1100 mL; capacities used in clinical diagnosis; spirometer for clinical assessment of pulmonary functions; BEYOND CHAPTER: vital capacity is higher in athletes

stem: State the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal breathing.
solution:
The volume of air that remains in the lungs after a normal expiration is the **Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)**.

FRC = **ERV + RV** = (1000-1100 mL) + (1100-1200 mL) = approximately **2100-2300 mL**.

Even after a forcible expiration, the **Residual Volume (RV)** of about 1100-1200 mL still remains in the lungs.
groundedIn: §14.2.1 — FRC is the volume of air that will remain in the lungs after a normal expiration, includes ERV+RV; ERV averages 1000-1100 mL; RV averages 1100-1200 mL

stem: Diffusion of gases occurs in the alveolar region only and not in the other parts of respiratory system. Why?
solution:
Only the **alveoli** (with their ducts) form the **respiratory or exchange part** of the respiratory system; the rest is only a **conducting part**.

1. The part from the external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles is the **conducting part**. It only transports atmospheric air to the alveoli, clears it of foreign particles, humidifies it and brings it to body temperature. The trachea, bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings and are not built for exchange.
2. **Alveoli** are very thin, irregular-walled and **vascularised** bag-like structures, richly supplied with blood capillaries.
3. The **diffusion membrane** between alveolar air and blood is made of only the thin squamous epithelium of the alveoli, the endothelium of the alveolar capillaries and the basement substance between them; its total thickness is much less than a millimetre.
4. A **partial pressure gradient** exists across this membrane: \(\text{pO}_2\) 104 mm Hg in alveoli against 40 mm Hg in deoxygenated blood, and \(\text{pCO}_2\) 45 mm Hg in deoxygenated blood against 40 mm Hg in alveoli.

Thus all the conditions favourable for diffusion of \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) are present only in the alveolar region.
groundedIn: §14.1.1; §14.3; Table 14.1; Fig. 14.4 — conducting part transports, clears, humidifies air; alveoli and their ducts form the exchange part, the site of actual diffusion; alveoli thin, irregular-walled, vascularised; diffusion membrane of three layers, much less than a millimetre; partial pressures in alveoli and blood

stem: What are the major transport mechanisms for \(\text{CO}_2\)? Explain.
solution:
\(\text{CO}_2\) is transported by blood in three ways: about **70 per cent as bicarbonate**, **20-25 per cent as carbamino-haemoglobin** in RBCs, and about **7 per cent dissolved in plasma**.

1. **As bicarbonate (about 70%):** RBCs contain a very high concentration of the enzyme **carbonic anhydrase** (minute quantities are present in plasma too), which catalyses the reaction in both directions:

\(\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}^+\) (both steps catalysed by carbonic anhydrase)

At the tissues, where \(\text{pCO}_2\) is high due to catabolism, \(\text{CO}_2\) diffuses into blood and forms \(\text{HCO}_3^-\) and \(\text{H}^+\). At the alveoli, where \(\text{pCO}_2\) is low, the reaction reverses, forming \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), and \(\text{CO}_2\) is released out.

2. **As carbamino-haemoglobin (20-25%):** \(\text{CO}_2\) binds to haemoglobin. When \(\text{pCO}_2\) is high and \(\text{pO}_2\) is low, as in the tissues, more binding occurs; when \(\text{pCO}_2\) is low and \(\text{pO}_2\) is high, as in the alveoli, \(\text{CO}_2\) dissociates and is delivered at the alveoli.

3. **Dissolved in plasma (about 7%).**

Every 100 ml of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately **4 ml of \(\text{CO}_2\)** to the alveoli.
groundedIn: §14.4; §14.4.2; Fig. 14.4 — 20-25 per cent of CO2 by RBCs, 70 per cent as bicarbonate, about 7 per cent dissolved in plasma; carbamino-haemoglobin binding depends on pCO2 and pO2; carbonic anhydrase reaction in both directions; 100 ml deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 ml CO2

stem: What will be the \(\text{pO}_2\) and \(\text{pCO}_2\) in the atmospheric air compared to those in the alveolar air ?
solution:
**(ii) \(\text{pO}_2\) higher, \(\text{pCO}_2\) lesser.**

| Gas | Atmospheric air | Alveoli |
|---|---|---|
| \(\text{O}_2\) | 159 mm Hg | 104 mm Hg |
| \(\text{CO}_2\) | 0.3 mm Hg | 40 mm Hg |

Atmospheric air has a higher \(\text{pO}_2\) (159 mm Hg) than alveolar air (104 mm Hg), and a much lower \(\text{pCO}_2\) (0.3 mm Hg) than alveolar air (40 mm Hg).
groundedIn: §14.3; Table 14.1 — partial pressures (mm Hg): O2 159 in atmospheric air, 104 in alveoli; CO2 0.3 in atmospheric air, 40 in alveoli

stem: Explain the process of inspiration under normal conditions.
solution:
**Inspiration** is the stage of breathing during which atmospheric air is drawn into the lungs. It occurs when the **intra-pulmonary pressure** becomes less than the atmospheric pressure, i.e., there is a negative pressure in the lungs.

1. Inspiration is initiated by the **contraction of the diaphragm**, which increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the **antero-posterior axis**.
2. Contraction of the **external inter-costal muscles** lifts up the ribs and the sternum, increasing the volume of the thoracic chamber in the **dorso-ventral axis**.
3. Since the thoracic chamber is air-tight and the lungs are set in it so that any change in thoracic volume is reflected in the lungs, the overall increase in thoracic volume causes a similar increase in **pulmonary volume**.
4. The increase in pulmonary volume **decreases the intra-pulmonary pressure** to less than the atmospheric pressure.
5. This pressure gradient forces air from outside to move into the lungs.

A healthy human breathes 12-16 times/minute, drawing in a tidal volume of about 500 mL in each normal inspiration.
groundedIn: §14.2; §14.1.1; Fig. 14.2; §14.2.1 — inspiration when intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric; contraction of diaphragm increases volume in antero-posterior axis; external intercostals lift ribs and sternum, dorso-ventral axis; thoracic chamber air-tight; 12-16 times/minute; tidal volume approx. 500 mL

solution:
Respiration is regulated by the **neural system**, which maintains and moderates the respiratory rhythm to suit the demands of the body tissues.

1. **Respiratory rhythm centre:** a specialised centre in the **medulla** region of the brain, primarily responsible for this regulation.
2. **Pneumotaxic centre:** present in the **pons** region; it moderates the functions of the respiratory rhythm centre. Its neural signal can reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate.
3. **Chemosensitive area:** situated adjacent to the rhythm centre and highly sensitive to \(\text{CO}_2\) and **hydrogen ions**. An increase in these activates it, and it signals the rhythm centre to adjust the respiratory process so that these substances are eliminated.
4. **Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery** also recognise changes in \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}^+\) concentration and send signals to the rhythm centre for remedial actions.

The role of **oxygen** in the regulation of respiratory rhythm is quite **insignificant**.
groundedIn: §14.5 — respiratory rhythm centre in medulla; pneumotaxic centre in pons reduces duration of inspiration; chemosensitive area sensitive to CO2 and H+; receptors of aortic arch and carotid artery; role of oxygen insignificant

stem: What is the effect of \(\text{pCO}_2\) on oxygen transport?
solution:
A **high \(\text{pCO}_2\)** favours the **dissociation of \(\text{O}_2\) from oxyhaemoglobin**, while a **low \(\text{pCO}_2\)** favours the **formation of oxyhaemoglobin**.

1. Binding of \(\text{O}_2\) with haemoglobin depends primarily on \(\text{pO}_2\); \(\text{pCO}_2\), \(\text{H}^+\) concentration and temperature also interfere with this binding.
2. **In the alveoli**, \(\text{pCO}_2\) is low (with high \(\text{pO}_2\), lesser \(\text{H}^+\) concentration and lower temperature), so the conditions favour the formation of **oxyhaemoglobin**, and \(\text{O}_2\) is loaded on the lung surface.
3. **In the tissues**, \(\text{pCO}_2\) is high (with low \(\text{pO}_2\), high \(\text{H}^+\) concentration and higher temperature), so the conditions favour **dissociation of \(\text{O}_2\)** from oxyhaemoglobin, and \(\text{O}_2\) is unloaded to the tissues.
4. On the oxygen dissociation curve, a rise in \(\text{pCO}_2\) shifts the curve to the **right** (lower affinity of haemoglobin for \(\text{O}_2\)); this is the **Bohr effect**.

Thus \(\text{pCO}_2\) helps \(\text{O}_2\) to be picked up at the lungs and released at the tissues.
groundedIn: §14.4.1; Fig. 14.5 — pCO2, H+ concentration and temperature interfere with O2 binding; in alveoli low pCO2 favours oxyhaemoglobin formation; in tissues high pCO2 favours dissociation; oxygen dissociation curve used to study effect of pCO2; BEYOND CHAPTER: a rise in pCO2 shifts the curve to the right (lower affinity), called the Bohr effect

stem: What happens to the respiratory process in a man going up a hill?
solution:
As a man goes up a hill, the **partial pressure of oxygen in the atmospheric air falls**, so less \(\text{O}_2\) reaches his tissues and his body compensates.

1. With lower atmospheric \(\text{pO}_2\), the \(\text{pO}_2\) of the alveolar air also falls, so the gradient for diffusion of \(\text{O}_2\) from alveoli to blood is reduced.
2. Binding of \(\text{O}_2\) with haemoglobin depends primarily on \(\text{pO}_2\), so less **oxyhaemoglobin** is formed and less \(\text{O}_2\) is delivered to the tissues.
3. To compensate, the **breathing rate and depth increase** (the person feels breathless) and the **heart beats faster**, so that more air and blood are moved per minute.
4. On a prolonged stay at high altitude, the body adjusts by producing more **RBCs and haemoglobin**, which raises the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood (acclimatisation).
groundedIn: §14.3; §14.4.1; Table 14.1 — O2 diffuses along a partial pressure gradient from alveoli to blood; binding of oxygen with haemoglobin is primarily related to pO2; BEYOND CHAPTER: atmospheric pO2 falls with altitude; breathing rate and depth and heart rate increase; prolonged stay raises RBC count and haemoglobin (acclimatisation)

stem: What is the site of gaseous exchange in an insect?
solution:
In an insect, gaseous exchange takes place directly at the **body tissues (cells)** through the **tracheal system**.

Insects have a network of tubes, the **tracheal tubes**, that transport atmospheric air within the body. Air enters through openings called **spiracles**, and the finest branches of the tubes (**tracheoles**) carry it right up to the cells, where \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) are exchanged by diffusion.
groundedIn: §14.1 — insects have a network of tubes (tracheal tubes) to transport atmospheric air within the body; BEYOND CHAPTER: air enters through spiracles; the finest branches (tracheoles) carry air to the cells, where gases are exchanged by diffusion

stem: Define oxygen dissociation curve. Can you suggest any reason for its sigmoidal pattern?
solution:
The **oxygen dissociation curve** is the sigmoid curve obtained when the **percentage saturation of haemoglobin with \(\text{O}_2\)** is plotted against the **\(\text{pO}_2\)**. It is useful in studying the effect of factors like \(\text{pCO}_2\) and \(\text{H}^+\) concentration on the binding of \(\text{O}_2\) with haemoglobin.

**Reason for the sigmoidal pattern:**

1. Each haemoglobin molecule can carry a maximum of **four molecules of \(\text{O}_2\)**.
2. Binding of the first \(\text{O}_2\) molecule makes it easier for the next ones to bind (**cooperative binding**). So at low \(\text{pO}_2\) saturation rises slowly, then rises **steeply** once binding begins.
3. At high \(\text{pO}_2\), as in the alveoli (104 mm Hg), nearly all binding sites are filled, so the curve **flattens** into a plateau.

The steep middle part lies around the tissue \(\text{pO}_2\) (40 mm Hg), so a small fall in \(\text{pO}_2\) there releases a large amount of \(\text{O}_2\) to the tissues.
groundedIn: §14.4.1; Fig. 14.5; Table 14.1 — sigmoid curve of percentage saturation of haemoglobin against pO2 is the oxygen dissociation curve; each haemoglobin molecule carries a maximum of four O2 molecules; pO2 104 mm Hg in alveoli, 40 mm Hg in tissues; BEYOND CHAPTER: cooperative binding (binding of the first O2 molecule raises haemoglobin's affinity for the next)

stem: Vital capacity and Total lung capacity.
solution:
| Basis | Vital Capacity (VC) | Total Lung Capacity (TLC) |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Maximum volume of air a person can **breathe in after a forced expiration** (or breathe out after a forced inspiration) | Total volume of air **accommodated in the lungs** at the end of a forced inspiration |
| Includes | **ERV + TV + IRV** | **RV + ERV + TV + IRV**, i.e., VC + RV |
| Residual volume | Not included | Included |
| Approximate value | about **4000-4600 mL** | about **5100-5800 mL** |
groundedIn: §14.2.1 — VC maximum volume breathed in after forced expiration, includes ERV, TV and IRV; TLC total volume accommodated in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration, includes RV, ERV, TV and IRV or VC + RV; volume values

stem: What is Tidal volume? Find out the Tidal volume (approximate value) for a healthy human in an hour.
solution:
**Tidal volume (TV)** is the volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration. It is approximately **500 mL**.

**Tidal volume in an hour:**

1. A healthy human breathes **12-16 times/minute**.
2. Volume per minute = 500 mL \(\times\) (12 to 16) = **6000 to 8000 mL/minute**.
3. Volume per hour = (6000 to 8000) mL \(\times\) 60 = **3,60,000 to 4,80,000 mL**, i.e., about **360 to 480 litres per hour**.
groundedIn: §14.2.1; §14.2 — tidal volume approx. 500 mL, a healthy man can inspire or expire approximately 6000 to 8000 mL of air per minute; a healthy human breathes 12-16 times/minute
